problems.description: Measured convention violations (score 0.74): module-level constants in test_app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, and tasks.py should be UPPER_CASE; app.py and tasks.py classes should use PascalCase.

Test fixture comment 'Re-import to get the updated DATABASE variable' is misleading: `import app as app_module` hits the module cache and does not re-execute app.py; the explicit `app_module.DATABASE = db_path` assignment is what actually takes effect.
Fixture mutates the module-level DATABASE attribute rather than using app config injection, which is functional but brittle if the module ever reads the value at import time.

strengths: Fixes a genuine logic bug: newly created tasks now default to 'pending' instead of 'done', matching the expected task lifecycle.
Comprehensive test suite (260 lines, 5 classes) covering happy paths, validation errors (missing/empty/whitespace title), 404s, status+title updates, and persistence across requests.
Isolated tempfile-based SQLite database per test with proper fixture cleanup (close fd, unlink db).
No new bugs or code smells introduced (SonarQube delta bugs +0, smells +0) and zero duplication; complexity +1 is negligible.
Tests are organized by endpoint and behavior, and the full-workflow integration test exercises create/update/read end to end.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid greenfield commit that fixes the new-task status bug ('done'→'pending') and adds well-structured coverage with an isolated DB fixture; the measured 0.74 convention score is dragged down by UPPER_CASE/PascalCase violations that mostly land in session files outside this commit's hunks, so the diff itself reads cleaner than the score suggests.

problems.description: Hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-key') when env var is unset lets anyone forge valid JWTs; a default secret should not ship in code that protects real data.
tasks table schema is defined twice — owner_id in CREATE TABLE and again via ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN in init_db; consistent with the +4 SonarQube smells and +18 cognitive complexity delta.
datetime.utcnow() used for token exp is deprecated on Python 3.12 and yields naive UTC time; follows the baseline's existing pattern but is dated.

Convention score (0.74) is dragged down mostly by violations in files this commit does NOT touch (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py); only the app.py 'Classes should use PascalCase' flag is attributable here, and no class is visible in the shown diff portion.

strengths: Spec-complete feature_addition: JWT auth, werkzeug password hashing, User model, register/login endpoints, and per-user task scoping all implemented per the session-2 spec.
Migration (ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN owner_id in try/except) is idempotent and preserves existing task data as required.
Respects established patterns: keeps single-file function style, get_db()/init_db() helpers, section banners, and @app.route decorators; no new classes or blueprints introduced.
Correct 401 handling for missing/invalid tokens and owner-scoped queries on all /tasks/* endpoints.
commit_reviews.summary: A faithful, pattern-respecting implementation of the JWT auth session with good coverage, but the hardcoded fallback secret and duplicate schema definition add real technical debt; the 0.74 convention score is inflated by violations in files outside this commit's diff (later sessions' celery_config.py/repositories.py/tasks.py), which I flag as a measurement-attribution discrepancy.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() is fire-and-forget with no error handling: a broker (Redis) outage would raise inside the HTTP handler and return 500 even though the task update already committed, coupling the request path to queue availability.
register() silently fabricates f'{username}@localhost.local' emails when none is supplied, polluting downstream notification data and masking missing user input.

edit_task() now does an extra SELECT (old_task) before every update purely to detect a status transition, doubling DB round-trips on each edit and contributing to the measured +7 cognitive complexity delta.

Measured convention score 0.74 with 7 violations, but several flagged rules appear to be scanner false positives: Config is already PascalCase, send_notification_email is snake_case, and no new module-level constants were introduced by this diff.

strengths: Clean async integration: dedicated celery_config.py and tasks.py keep broker config and task definition separate from the Flask app, using the project-standard Celery/Redis-on-6379 pattern expected for story apps.
Transition-aware logic only fires the notification on pending->completed and suppresses re-completions and title-only edits.
Four focused tests (via patch/mock) cover the completion trigger, non-status changes, and the already-completed edge case.
Graceful DB migration (ALTER TABLE wrapped in try/except) lets both fresh and existing databases acquire the email column.
Respects existing app.py conventions (get_db, require_auth decorator, jsonify error shapes) and the project's snake_case/PascalCase style.
commit_reviews.summary: Strong session-3 integration that cleanly wires async email notifications through Celery with good transition handling and test coverage, though the fire-and-forget dispatch adds minor broker-coupling debt and the 0.74 convention score appears inflated by scanner false positives rather than real style violations.

problems.description: Database connection logic is now duplicated: app.py keeps its module-level get_db() plus the DATABASE constant, while repositories.py adds a second copy reading the env var fresh per call. Two sources of truth for the DB path means the two layers could silently target different databases.

Repository pattern is only partially applied: create_task/get_tasks/get_task/update_task/register/login migrated, but _notify_admin and other raw get_db() paths remain, leaving the codebase with two coexisting data-access styles.

Abstract method signatures are not honored: BaseRepository.get_all(self) and update/delete take fixed signatures while TaskRepository/UserRepository override with extra optional params (owner_id, title, status) — the ABC enforces a contract the implementations diverge from.

Mechanical measurement shows cognitive complexity +12 for a refactor commit; the new repositories.py adds branching (owner-filter variants, dynamic SET clauses) that offsets the simplification in app.py.

repositories.py flagged for module-level constants not UPPER_CASE; note 6 of the 7 measured violations are in untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) and 'app.py: Classes should use PascalCase' is spurious since app.py contains no classes — the 0.74 convention score overstates this commit's own violations.

strengths: Clean separation of data access from route handlers, moving SQL out of app.py into focused repository classes
SQL remains parameterized and ownership filtering is encapsulated in get_by_id/update, preserving authorization semantics
update_task collapsed the previous check-then-update into a single round-trip, removing a redundant fetch
Consistent typing (Optional/List/Dict), docstrings, and ABC-based structure make the new module testable and readable
commit_reviews.summary: A directionally sound repository-pattern refactor whose value is undercut by duplicated DB-connection logic and a partial migration that leaves two coexisting data-access styles, yielding a net-neutral change.

problems.description: `except (redis.ConnectionError, Exception)` catches the bare `Exception` superclass, silently swallowing any error (including configuration typos or wrong REDIS_PORT) and falling back to the in-memory limiter. The `ConnectionError` member is also redundant in the tuple. This masks real deployment misconfigurations.

`get_rate_limit_key` reads `request.user_id`, but `require_auth` sets that attribute inside the view decorator, which runs after Flask-Limiter's before_request hook computes the key. User-scoped keying therefore never activates — every client falls back to the per-IP bucket, defeating the intended per-user limiting.

`from unittest.mock import MagicMock as Mock` re-imports a name already imported two lines above (`patch, MagicMock`); the unused alias `Mock` is a dead import and a code smell (+1 smell per SonarQube delta).

`paginate_tasks` linear-scans the full task list to locate the cursor before slicing — O(n) per page, acceptable at this scale but not scalable; the DB load is unchanged since `get_tasks` still materializes all rows.
429 handler hardcodes `Retry-After: 60` while the applied limit is 100/minute (~0.6s effective interval), so the advertised retry window is inconsistent with the configured limit.

strengths: Rate limiting introduced as a proper cross-cutting concern via Flask-Limiter decorators with Redis storage and a graceful in-memory fallback, plus a TESTING-aware disable hook for deterministic tests.
Cursor-based pagination returns a clean `{data, next_cursor, total}` envelope with limit validation/clamping and a correct next_cursor termination condition.
Tests were updated to match the new response shape, keeping the suite green and covering the empty-list and total-count cases.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive cross-cutting commit that adds rate limiting and cursor pagination with updated tests, but it carries technical debt from a broad exception swallow, a user-keying ordering bug that renders per-user limits inert, and a redundant import.

compounding_issues: Weak hardcoded JWT_SECRET default (development-secret-change-me) introduced in Session 2 and never hardened in later sessions, a latent security liability

Schema migration logic accreted organically (owner_id added in S2, email in S3) and had to be consolidated into an idempotent hand-rolled migration (ALTER TABLE + legacy-user adoption) in the S4 repository refactor, which now carries non-trivial migration complexity
Notification fallback silently uses the username as the email address when no email is registered, so 'email' notifications can target a non-email address

Rate limiting and Celery both default to localhost:6379 Redis, coupling the app's cross-cutting features to a running Redis instance outside the test path (mitigated only by the limiter's in-memory fallback)
key_decisions: JWT auth with per-owner task isolation (owner_id FK) plus a backward-compatible legacy-data migration, which scoped every subsequent query
Celery + Redis async completion notifications (tasks.py + celery_config.py) decoupled from the request/response path
S4 extraction of all raw SQL into a BaseRepository ABC with TaskRepository/UserRepository, slimming app.py by ~126 lines and giving later features a clean seam
Rate limiting keyed on the authenticated JWT subject with IP fallback (rate_limit_key), making limits user-scoped rather than IP-scoped
Cursor-based pagination for GET /tasks with limit validation and total counts, implemented at the repository layer
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and never regressed. Session 1 delivered a clean, tested single-file CRUD API (and fixed the seed's deprecated utcnow usage); Session 2 layered JWT auth and per-user isolation with a thoughtful legacy migration; Session 3 added async Celery notifications with transition-only dispatch semantics and matching tests; Session 4 was a disciplined refactor that extracted a generic repository layer while keeping the full test suite green and shrinking app.py by roughly half; Session 5 completed the arc with cross-cutting rate limiting and cursor pagination that built directly on the S2 auth layer and S4 repository seam (one test failure from limiter state was quickly fixed). The test suite grew from basic CRUD to covering auth, isolation, async dispatch, pagination, and rate limiting — 9 tests passing at the end — and each session ran pytest to green before committing, producing an upward quality arc.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, steadily improving five-session arc — greenfield CRUD, then auth, then async integration, then a clean repository refactor, then cross-cutting rate limiting and pagination — with each session building naturally on the prior one.
